title: Cloud Platform Services
html:
Cloud Platform Services

Written against Azure's naming, but the shapes are the same on any major cloud. What matters is the decision each service represents.

Where code runs

Option Model Fits
Virtual machine you manage the OS legacy, or unusual OS needs
App service managed web host a normal web application
Container service you ship an image consistent environments, mixed stacks
Orchestrator many containers, scheduled many services, real scale
Functions event-triggered, per-execution spiky or occasional work

The trade is control against operational burden. Each step up the list is less to manage and less to tune. The common mistake is choosing an orchestrator for two services, then spending the year on the orchestrator.

Serverless cold starts are the caveat: an idle function pays initialisation on the next call. Fine for a nightly job, poor for an interactive path with a latency budget.

Where data lives

  • Relational, managed - a normal database with backups, patching and failover handled. The default.
  • Document store - flexible shape, horizontal scale, and a consistency model you must actually choose.
  • Blob/object storage - files. Cheap, tiered by access frequency, not a database.
  • Cache - in-memory, for hot reads and sessions.
  • Queue or bus - decoupling producers from consumers, with retry and dead-lettering.

Pick per workload rather than per project. One relational database and one object store covers a surprising amount.

Identity

A managed identity directory issues tokens; the application validates them and reads claims. The point of interest is that a workload can have an identity of its own, so a service reaches a database or a secret store without any credential in configuration. That removes the whole class of leaked connection strings, and it is worth restructuring for.

Role assignments should be scoped as narrowly as the work allows. A subscription-wide contributor role granted for convenience is the thing that turns one compromised component into a whole-environment incident.

Secrets and configuration

Application settings for the non-secret, a managed secret store for the rest, with access by workload identity rather than a key. Rotate on a schedule and after any suspicion. A secret in a repository is compromised the moment it is pushed, whatever the repository's visibility.

Messaging

Queues give at-least-once delivery, which means handlers must be idempotent - the same message may arrive twice and processing it twice must be harmless. Design for it rather than hoping.

Dead-letter queues catch what repeatedly fails. Left unmonitored they become a silent hole where work disappears; alert on depth.

Cost and reliability

The two things that surprise teams:

Egress and cross-region traffic are charged, and are easy to incur accidentally by placing a service in a different region from its data. Co-locate.

Availability zones protect against a datacentre failure; regions protect against a regional one, at the cost of latency and replication complexity. Decide which you are actually buying, and test the failover - an untested failover is a hypothesis.

Common mistakes

  • Choosing an orchestrator before the complexity justifies it.
  • Credentials in configuration where a workload identity would do.
  • Over-broad role assignments granted to unblock something and never narrowed.
  • No budget alert, and discovering the cost at the end of the month.
  • Serverless on a latency-sensitive path without measuring cold starts.
